# Copper June 2010 

- In the absence of any meaningful fundamental market news copper’s fortunes were driven almost entirely by macroeconomic events during June.  Volatile trading conditions remained much in evidence with, for example, 3m prices plummeting earlier in the month by almost $550/t over three consecutive trading days before settling at $6123/t on the 8th.  Most of this loss was recouped by the 15th, although this soon ran out of steam following a wave of Chinese profit-taking on the 17th.  Since then the 3m quotes have trended broadly upwards reaching a monthly high of $6826/t on the 28th.  However, prices have since retraced somewhat and are currently trading around $6640/t. 

- As the main engine of global consumption, it goes without saying that the relative health of China’s economy is critical to copper’s fortunes.  It is also clear that recent growth rates in many of China’s end-use markets have been unsustainable and there is now increasing evidence of a major slowdown in the pace of growth in a number of these sectors.  Another concern for market participants is that Chinese exports of copper semi products may fall following news that China is to abolish its 5% tax rebate on certain copper semi products from mid July. 

- For this year through to 2012 we have raised our global demand forecasts by a net 31kt, 125kt and 34kt respectively. The net increases primarily reflect higher than previously expected Chinese demand in this year.  This follows the recent news that China’s home appliance subsidy scheme is to be extended to the end of 2012.  Previously it was due to end last month.  Thus we now expect global refined copper consumption to increase by 6.1% this year, to ~18.3Mt, by 6.8% in 2011 to ~19.6Mt and by 3.4% in 2012 to ~20.2Mt. 

- According to trade rumour it appears that BHP Billiton, acting on behalf of Escondida has concluded its first mid-year deal during its third round discussions with South Korea’s LS Nikko.  Terms are thought to have been agreed at $39/t & 3.9c/lb.  The Chilean miner’s next discussions will be with Indian buyers and there is a strong likelihood that more settlements will be established at this level of TC/RCs.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Mixed trading patterns continue through June** In the absence of any meaningful fundamental market news copper’s fortunes were driven almost entirely by macro-economic events during June.  Volatile trading conditions remained much in evidence with, for example, 3m prices plummeting earlier in the month by almost $550/t over three consecutive trading days before settling at $6123/t on the 8<sup>th</sup> .  The subsequent rally saw most of this loss recouped by the 15<sup>th</sup> , although this soon ran out of steam following a wave of Chinese profit-taking after participants returned from their “Dragon Boat Race” holiday on the 17<sup>th</sup> .  Since then the market has regained some of its composure with 3m quotes trending broadly upwards and reaching a monthly high of $6826/t on the 28<sup>th</sup> .  However, prices have since retraced somewhat and are currently trading around $6640/t. 

**Market sentiment dampened during the first week** Several factors were responsible for the poor start to June that led to a decline in prices during the first week of the month.  The most significant of these included growing concerns over the spectre of slower Chinese demand growth, fuelled by weakening Chinese economic data, deteriorating economic data releases from the US, and renewed concerns over the European sovereign debt crisis.  Perhaps the main indicator that sparked concerns over Chinese economic/copper demand growth was the country’s Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) which fell from 55.7 in April to 53.9 in May.  After an exceptionally strong start to the year many feared that the impact of China’s recent tightening policy measures were starting to feed through the system to the detriment of copper demand growth.  Meanwhile in the US, non-farm payrolls fell in April but the decline was not as strong as many had expected.  Finally, concerns over Europe’s debt crisis were reignited on the 7<sup>th</sup> with Hungary declaring its financial difficulties.  This news prompted massive long liquidation which resulted in official 3-month quotes falling by $300/t on the 7<sup>th</sup> to $6181/t, the month’s largest daily decline. 

**Prices supported by several factors** Between the 9<sup>th</sup> and the 15<sup>th</sup> official 3-month quotes recovered strongly, rising from $6123/t on the 8<sup>th</sup> to $6654/t on the 15<sup>th</sup> .  Prices rallied by over $130/t on three of the five trading days.  The bounce back in prices was particularly robust on the 9<sup>th</sup> with official quotes rising by $193/t to $$6315/t.  Firmer equity markets (perhaps the result of improved risk appetite) were primarily responsible for the rebound and this was exaggerated by short position holders rushing to cover their exposure.  The release of positive provisional Chinese trade data and a stronger Euro also provided market support during these five days.  However, the release of negative US economic data

, Chinese selling and renewed concerns over Europe’s debt crisis, between the 16th and 18th dampened sentiment again with prices falling by $317/t over the three-day period to $6338/t on the 18th . In the US, unemployment and housing data was not as strong as expected while in Europe there were rumours that an emergency credit line for Spain was being put in place by the EU, IMF and the US Treasury. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

**Revaluation of the Chinese yuan** On the 19th the People’s Bank of China announced that it would “enhance the renminbi exchange rate flexibility”. The announcement (impeccably timed a week ahead of the G20 summit) sparked a brief rally across base metal markets, with market watchers predicting that any appreciation of the renminbi would be a boost to Chinese metal imports, and fundamentally positive for prices (see Economic Focus). As a consequence official 3-month prices jumped $307/t on the day to $6645/t. However, prices corrected the following day, falling by $155/t to $6489/t on the 22nd . While the initial market reaction to the announcement was positive, the reality of the situation then became clearer, i.e. with the appreciation of the renminbi likely to come at a very slow rate, and trade flows typically slow to react to exchange rate shifts, any changes in metals demand trends and prices would most likely be gradual. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2010 Page 2 of 24 Copper Monthly Update **Exchange stocks continue to decline** Total exchange stocks decreased in June for the second consecutive month. Inventories fell by a net 57.3kt, to 668.4kt, as of the 28th . Net withdrawals were recorded on both the LME and SHFE while stocks in Comex warehouses were relatively unchanged at 92.5kt. Inventories in Shanghai warehouses fell by a net 33.8kt, to 124kt, while LME stocks were reduced by a net 23.6kt to 452kt. This represented the fourth consecutive month of decline for LME warrants and was not surprising in light of Q2 typically being the strongest quarter with regards to demand. Similar to May, the largest withdrawals in LME warrants occurred in the US where inventories fell by a net 9.1kt to 309kt. Once again the largest decline occurred in New Orleans where inventories fell by a net 8kt to 180.4kt. Meanwhile in Europe, stocks were reduced by a net 5.6kt to 57kt. Withdrawals mainly took place from warehouses in Rotterdam (-1.3kt), Bilbao (-2.1kt) and Liverpool (-1.6kt). At the time of writing (the 29th ) LME cance

lled warrants totalled 31.2kt, indicating that further withdrawals should continue to take place in the coming weeks. **European spot business very quiet** According to trade sources very little European spot activity has taken place during the month. That said despite the low activity levels spot premia have remained firm at last month’s levels. One trader noted that this reflected availability problems, which resulted from vessel delays, rather than any pick-up in underlying demand. For example, Italian cathode consumers were forced into the spot market during the month because of delayed vessels from Chile. It should be borne in mind that many consumers are operating on a hand-to-mouth basis so any delay in cathode will result in spot purchases in order to meet commitments. Italian warrants have thus continued to trade at $85/t. Elsewhere, Chilean and grade A cathode from Rotterdam continued to fetch between $70-80/t while standard grade material remained at $20/t above LME quotes. **US premia move higher** Premia in the US increased during the month, rising from 4-4.5c/lb in May to 4.5-5.5c/lb presently. As was the case last month, premia continued to be supported by tight scrap availability. We hear that some copper semi fabricators were forced to buy cathode from the spot market because they were unable to source scrap. As we noted in our last monthly report, some scrap traders have held material back from the market awaiting higher copper prices while the general malaise in the industrial demolition market persists. Premia were also supported this month by reduced truck availability because of high agricultural produce demand. **Chinese premia strengthen** Chinese premia strengthened during June, rising from $80-100/t in May to $120-130/t presently. The increase reflected favourable arbitrage conditions and tighter supply of Japanese material. While there is material available for immediate delivery from LME warehouses in South Korea and Singapore, very little of this is believed to be of premium quality. Because of this Chinese consumers have preferred to source better quality material from Japanese producers. However, availability of Japanese spot material has been limited of late due to rising consumption requirements from domestic contract customers, which Japanese producers are obligated to cover, on the back of a much stronger-than-expected Japanese copper demand (see Consumption). #### **Copper Spot Premia ($/t)** 200 W Europe Shanghai US c/lb 10.0

**Shanghai arbitrage conditions remain favourable** SHFE/LME arbitrage conditions remained favourable during June, especially during the latter part of the month with LME quotes trading an ave

rage $159/t below SHFE prices (exclusive of VAT), between the 21st and the 29th . Thus far in June LME quotes averaged $55/t below SHFE prices (exclusive of VAT) through to the 29th . This was not dissimilar to last month when LME quotes traded an average $67/t below SHFE prices. During H1 the SHFE/LME arbitrage traded in favour of the SHFE in all months barring March and April. As we noted in our last monthly report, all things being equal, we would expect to see a rise in refined imports over the next four to six weeks (this being the normal lead time between metal being booked and when it arrives in China, unless material is Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2010 Page 3 of 24 Copper Monthly Update shipped directly from Chinese bonded warehouses) on account of the favourable arbitrage conditions in both May and June. **Chinese refined imports fall for the second consecutive month in May** According to latest trade data Chinese refined imports continued their downward trend in May having fallen by 9.7% from a month earlier to ~280kt. This followed a month-on-month decline of 8.1% in April to 310kt. The reduction was expected on account of unfavourable arbitrage conditions during April when SHFE prices traded an average $147/t below LME quotes. However, as noted previously, improved arbitrage conditions in May and June could translate into a rise in imports over the coming month or so. Any increase may also reflect reduced flows of scrap following the recent implementation of a new scrap import policy that commenced on the 1st of this month (see our May report). #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 Refined Imports 400

**Concerns over Chinese demand growth** As the main engine of global consumption, it goes without saying that the relative health of China’s economy is critical to copper’s fortunes. It is also clear that recent growth rates in many of China’s end-use markets have been unsustainable and there is now increasing evidence of a major slowdown in the pace of growth in a number of these sectors. Another concern for market participants is that Chinese exports of copper semi products may fall following news that China is to abolish its 5% tax rebate on certain copper semi products from mid July. However, we hear that the removal of the tax will have no impact on the level of copper semi products exported because most of the export business is carried out on a tolling basis for which the tax is not applicable. Semi fabricators prefer to conduct their export business on a tolling basis because it enables them to avoid paying 17.5% VAT on their imported cathode purchases. In

gauging the relative overall health of Chinese copper demand, comparisons of apparent refined consumption are relatively meaningless at present due to the large accumulation of speculative and strategic inventories during 2009. That said according to China’s Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNIA) China’s copper semis production recorded a very respectable increase of 12% year-on-year in May compared with a cumulative figure to date of 19%. Also, power cable production is reported to have increased by 24% year-on-year in May while the uplift in output of power equipment and power generating capacity were 17% and 19% respectively over the same period. Another positive is the extension of the home appliance subsidy scheme which thus far this year has been a major support to copper demand (see Consumption). This, combined with China’s plans to encourage the production of electric vehicles and the ongoing upgrade the country’s power infrastructure, both of which are copper intensive, will serve to support Chinese copper demand in the near-to medium-term. Thus we forecast that Chinese refined copper consumption will increase by 10% this year, to ~7.2Mt, 8% in 2011 and 5% in 2012 to ~7.8Mt and 8.1Mt, respectively. **Market surplus considerably reduced in 2010** The strong growth in Chinese demand this year is largely responsible for supporting our estimate of 6% growth in global refined copper consumption to ~18.3Mt. Refined production is forecast to increase by just 0.5% to 18.4Mt which will result in global market “surplus” of ~150kt. This is down considerably from the 1.1Mt accumulated in 2009. Our average price for this year is forecast to increase by 30.1% to $6726/t ($3.05/lb). **Full demand recovery expected in 2011** In 2011 a full recovery in underlying demand is expected, alongside improving construction activity, with global refined consumption forecast to rise by 6.8% to ~19.6Mt. While we project a meaningful increase in refined production (+5%, to 19.4Mt) this will not be sufficient to outweigh growth in demand. Thus the market should return to deficit (~-155kt) for the first time since 2006. Despite this, average prices are forecast to decline by 4.8% to $6400/t ($2.90/lb) reflecting our expectation of further “investment bleed-out” from commodities. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2010 Page 5 of 24 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Focus **Renminbi Rising: Back to the Future?** The People’s Bank of China (PBoC) announced on June 19th that it would “enhance the renminbi exchange rate flexibility”, effectively ending the Chinese currency’s peg to the US dollar. The announcement sparked a brief rally across base metal markets, with market watchers predicting that the appreciation of the renminbi would be a boost to Chinese metal imports, and fundamentally positive for prices. Whilst there are reasons to suggest that an appreciation on the renminbi is supportive of metal prices, it is important not to overestimate the impact of this development. #### **Chinese renminbi versus US dollar exchange rate and trade weighted index** 8.5 $US rate 120

The political implications of China’s announcement should be noted as it came a week before the G20 summit in Toronto, where the undervaluation of the renminbi was one of the key topics. By announcing increased flexibility in its exchange rate, China has managed to shift the attention away from its undervalued currency for the moment, without providing any guidance on when and by how much it would allow the renminbi to rise. #### **Wood Mackenzie’s renminbi/dollar exchange rate forecast** 9.0

**Appreciation will be slow** Any change in the Chinese exchange rate is likely to come slowly. When the currency peg was aband

oned and a trading band was first introduced in 2005, the market estimated a 5% appreciation over the coming 12 months. As it turns out, the PBoC allowed it appreciate just 3.5% in the first year, moving very slowly after the Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2010 Page 6 of 24 Copper Monthly Update initial adjustment. This time, expectations are more muted on the back of the 2005 example; the non-deliverable forwards market (financial instruments that are used where currency conversions are restricted) is currently pricing in a 2% appreciation over the next 12 months. In a follow up statement on June 20th , the PBoC stated that a substantial appreciation was not in China’s interests, and that the exchange rate would remain basically stable. Pressure for China to allow the renminbi to appreciate faster has been lessened somewhat by the weakness of the euro – a weakness that we expect to persist for a prolonged period. As the chart above shows, the renminbi has already been appreciating on a trade weighted basis since late 2009, and the structural weakness of the euro will continue to buoy the renminbi. Wood Mackenzie expects only a very slight appreciation of the renminbi in 2010, and a further 3% gain in both 2011 and 2012. **Implications for metals** When considering the implication of possible changes in China’s exchange rate policy for the metal markets and prices, there are four key points. Firstly, at the most basic level, an appreciation of the renminbi against the dollar makes $US priced assets, such as base metal imports, relatively less expensive for Chinese buyers. This is akin to the inverse relationship the dollar has with metal prices, where a weaker dollar results in higher metal prices. Cheaper metal prices for Chinese buyers results in lower production or capital costs for many industries in China, which could transfer to lower end-product prices for items such as cars, stimulating additional demand over the longer term. All other things being equal, higher demand results in higher metal prices. In terms of base metals, one would expect the greatest impact would be felt in those metals where Chinese imports account for a larger share of the total market, such as copper and nickel. 2009 Chinese refined metal net imports 2009 net imports as a percentage of global demand

Conversely, the stronger renminbi makes exports of metals and metal products more expensive in $US terms. For concentrates and refined metals, the impact should be limited, as China is for the most part a net importer. It would be felt more in metal containing products that China exports in large volumes, such as industrial parts, and would resu

lt in a loss of competitiveness for Chinese exporters.  We could, for example, see China less competitive versus Germany in global export markets in high-end manufactured goods. 

**Higher marginal costs** Thirdly, an appreciation of the renminbi will also push Chinese producers higher up the cost curve.  This is particularly important in aluminium, zinc and lead, where many Chinese producers are already in upper quartile of the cost curve.  A stronger renminbi could potentially raise the marginal cost of production in these metals, raising the cyclical floor price.  Of course, this could be offset somewhat by lower raw material input costs for those using imported ores or with other $US denominated costs. 

**Appreciation results in tighter monetary conditions** The last, and perhaps most important, issue is the implication of a renminbi appreciation on China’s, and indeed the rest of the world’s, economic growth.  Fundamentally speaking, to keep a currency artificially low, a country must increase the supply of it.  China has maintained its exchange rate by printing renminbi and using them to buy dollars, resulting in the PBoC accumulating large foreign exchange reserves, but also increasing liabilities, including domestic currency.  Reducing the extent to which it intervenes in the foreign exchange markets effectively results in monetary contraction, which has negative implications for Chinese investment and thus metals demand. 

It has been argued that a shift to a flexible exchange rate policy in China would help to rebalance global trade problems, reducing excessive consumption in trade deficit countries like the USA and boosting consumption in China.  This may well be the case, but Chinese growth driven more by the domestic consumer and less by exporting companies would be a shift away from the capital investment intensive, and thus metals intensive, model of growth that has been prevalent in recent years.  Ultimately, increased flexibility in China’s exchange rate is not in itself going to solve the global economic problems.  With the appreciation of the renminbi likely to come at a very slow rate, and trade flows typically slow to react to exchange rate shifts, any changes in metals demand trends and prices will be gradual.  Individual market fundamentals will continue to be the main driver of price.

## Consumption 

**Indian demand for 2009 revised lower** We have made a series of amendments to our demand forecasts for this year, 2011 and 2012 since our last monthly report.  On the downside we have lowered our Indian figures by ~50kt in 2010, ~65kt in 2011 and 95kt in 2012.  The weaker forecasts reflect a 40kt reduction to our 2009 demand estimate following the release of final reported consumption data for last year which was not as high as we had expected.  In contrast, official data recently reported for last year indicated that our 2009 Sou

th Korean demand estimate was too low which led us to increase it by 34kt. This upward revision, combined with a few minor upward amendments to our European forecasts, offset the reduction in our 2009 Indian demand estimate. Thus, we continue to estimate that global refined copper consumption decreased to 17.2Mt in 2009, down 3.8% from a year earlier. **Near term demand forecasts increased** For this year through to 2012 we have raised our global demand forecasts by a net 31kt, 125kt and 34kt respectively. The net increases primarily reflect higher than previously expected Chinese demand in this year. This follows the recent news that China’s home appliance subsidy scheme is to be extended to the end of 2012. Previously it was due to end at the end may 2010. Thus we now expect global refined copper consumption to increase by 6.1% this year, to ~18.3Mt, by 6.8% in 2011, to ~19.6Mt and by 3.4% in 2012 to ~20.2Mt. ### **China** **China’s output of white goods surge** Chinese demand for white goods remains firm, helped by the government’s subsidy scheme for home appliances. In February last year the Chinese government launched the subsidy programme to spur consumption of home appliances, particularly in rural areas, which, in turn, helped buoy economic growth amid the global economic downturn. The success of the programme was highlighted by the Ministry of Commerce, which reported a 510% surge in the domestic sales of home appliances during the first four months of this year from the corresponding period in 2010. In April alone, 4.8M sets of subsidised home appliances were sold, according to the government department. This represented an annual increase of 170%. The scheme covers home appliances such as refrigerators, television sets, washing machines, air conditioner units, mobile phones, water heaters, micro-wave ovens and normal ovens. Reflecting the surge in home appliance sales, the National Bureau of Statistics reported that the output of washing machines, refrigerators, freezers and air conditioner units increased annually by 37.9%, 29.3%, 36% and 38.6% respectively during the first five months of the year. Such strong output growth helped support demand for copper and copper alloys which increased by ~19.2% year-on-year during the same 5-month period, according to China’s Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNIA). Also positive was the recent news that the Chinese government has decided to extend the home appliance subsidy scheme. Initially the scheme was due to finish at the end of May but it has now been extended until the end of this year. We have raised our Chinese demand forecasts to reflect this and now expect Chinese refined copper consumption to increase by 10% this year, to ~7.2Mt, and by 8% in 2011 to ~7.8Mt. #### **Chinese production of copper and copper alloy products – (kt)** 50 % change Production 3000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2010 Page 8 of 24 Copper Monthly Update ### **South Korea** **The recovery in the South Korean economy is divided** Manufacturing activity has remained firm in South Korea where large exporters have performed particularly well. This has been supported by the auto sector where production has remained relatively strong despite the government-supported automotive programme having finished at the end of 2009. Auto production fell in January but recovered in February and March to total 897k units for the quarter as a whole. This was up 41% from a year earlier and was only marginally below pre-crisis levels. However, domestic vehicle sales have not been able to reach the levels achieved during the automotive programme in 2009 and have averaged just 99k units per month through the first four months of 2010. This compared with sales of 111k units per month from May to December last year. Thus export demand is largely responsible for supporting the ongoing growth in South Korean auto production. **The South Korean construction market is also showing strong signs of recovery** South Korea’s construction sector is also reported to be performing well. According to latest government statistics floor space under construction for dwellings jumped in March to 3176m2 which brought the overall total for Q1 level with Q1 in 2008 i.e before the global downturn in construction activity took hold. Commercial floor space under construction also improved sharply in March, where it rose by 25% year on year to 2524m2 . **Strong wire rod demand** According to our sources domestic demand for copper wire rod is healthy, reflecting firm orders from both the auto and construction sectors. Domestic demand from the electrical and electronic sector is also reported to be robust as South Korea’s export market for electrical and electronic goods remains positive. Our sources also informed us that export demand for copper wire rod is holding up. Latest trade data showed that exports of copper wire rod totalled 45kt during the first four months of the year, up 1% from the same period in 2009. While this may not seem such a strong gain, it follows on from substantial growth recorded in 2009 where wire rod exports surged 41.8% (+43.5kt) to 147.6kt. Of course, China was the main destination, where exports totalled 89.5kt, up 43% (+26.9kt) from 2008. We estimate that South Korean refined copper consumption increased by 5.9% last year to ~785kt. ### **India** 

**India buoyed by domestic market** India has managed to weather the economic storm of the past 18 months, reflecting healthy levels of domestic demand.  This recovery in domestic demand has encouraged a surge in capacity utilisation and prompted a pick up in private sector investment, both from domestic and foreign sources.  Robust manufacturing

activity has also provided economic support, with the manufacturing purchasing manager’s index for May rose from 57.2 in April to 59.  The new orders component of the index, which rose from 61.9 to 63.7, was particularly encouraging. India’s strong economic activity will support copper consumption growth, particularly as a significant portion of the surge in investment has been in new construction where investment increased by 8.7% in Q1 from a year earlier.  Reflecting this we forecast that Indian refined copper consumption will increase by 6.5% this year to ~590kt.  In 2011 further growth of 8.3% is expected to ~640kt.  The stronger growth will primarily reflect ongoing investment within the country’s power infrastructure as well as continued growth within the country’s construction sector. 

### **Brazil** 

**Brazil protected by domestic demand** Similar to India, Latin America’s largest economy has weathered the economic downturn because of its developed domestic market.  However, the pace of expansion has been so great that Brazil’s central bank moved to increase interest rates by 75 basis points in June, the second increase this year.  This has taken the overnight lending rate to 10.3%.  Additional interest rate increases are expected during the year as inflation remains above the bank’s 4.5% target rate.  There are some suggestions that the rate may reach 12% by the end of the year. 

**Automotive sector is performing well** Brazil’s automotive sector is growing at a healthy rate, with year-on-year growth in car pro

duction moderating from the 32% seen in January to 0.3% in May.  Production for the first five months totalled 1.05M units, up 8.6% from the corresponding period in 2009.  Sales, which posted double digit growth earlier in the year because of a sales tax abatement, have now returned to more normal levels. 

**Brazilian copper demand remains healthy** Brazil’s demand for copper has benefitted from the buoyant automotive sector.  The forthcoming moves to upgrade the nation’s infrastructure in the run-up to the 2014 FIFA World Cup and the 2016 Summer Olympics will provide further support to demand growth.  The government’s plans to upgrade the country’s power network will also provide support to future refined copper demand.  Thus we forecast that Brazilian refined copper demand will increase by 4% this year, to 350kt, and by a stronger 9.1% in 2011 to just below 390kt. 

### **Japan** 

**Japan’s recovery in copper semi products continues** Demand for copper and copper alloy products continued its recovery during April.  Production of copper semi products increased by 66.8% year-on-year in April, according to the Japan Copper and Brass Manufacturers Association.  This represented the sixth consecutive month of annual increase. However, the sharp rise should be taken in context with last year’s very poor performance where production in April declined by ~49% from a year earlier.  A better indication of how well the recovery is doing would be to compare current production levels with output in 2008 i.e. prior to the global financial crisis.  Thus, production in copper semi products in April this year, at 74.1kt, was down 14.2% (-12.3kt) from April in 2008.  However, we expect that this negative growth will narrow in the coming months as Japanese demand for copper and copper alloy products continues to recover.  Indeed provisional data recently released for May showed that this was already the case where the production of copper semi products in May fell by 12% from output levels recorded in May 2008. 

**Demand for copper and brass strip lead the recovery** According to the Japan Copper and Brass Manufacturers Association the production of copper and brass strip increased by 56.7kt (+184%) and 27.6kt (+236%) to 87.5kt and 39kt respectively during the first four months of the year from the corresponding period in 2009.  Both products are now only marginally away from pre-crisis levels.  The recovery in the copper strip market reflects improving demand from both the domestic and export markets for consumer electronics (especially in China) and autos.  Latest data available showed that Japanese auto production increased by 56% in April from a year earlier.  Healthy orders from these two sectors also provided support to the production of brass bar which increased by 43.6% (+18.9kt) during Jan-Apr year-on-year, according to the Association.  The increase was not as strong as the recovery in copper and brass strip because of ongoing weak demand from the co

nstruction sector in the form of water taps and gas appliances.  Elsewhere, the Association reported that the production of copper tube increased annually by 15.5% (+5.7kt) during the first four months of the year.  The recovery reflected increased demand for residential air conditioners. 

**Shipments of copper wire and cable continue to increase** Demand for copper wire and cable also continued to be supported by improving orders from both the auto and electrical and electronic sectors.  According to the Japan Cable Makers Association, shipments to these two sectors increased by 63.4% and 53.3% respectively during the first four months of the year.  Overall, the Association reported that shipments of wire and cable increased by 10% during Jan-Apr from a year earlier.  The lower growth rate, compared with the recovery in deliveries of automotive and electrical and electronic wire and cable, reflected depressed demand for wire and cable from the construction, telecommunication and power sectors.  Wire and cable shipments to these sectors during the first four months of the year fell by 10.4% (-10.3kt), 10.9% (-0.7kt) and 7.1% (-1.7kt respectively).  While the recovery in both the wire and cable and copper and copper alloy product markets is encouraging, concern that the economy will be slow to recover fully remains.  This stems from persistent deflation (which is expected to continue for the next two years), ongoing weak activity from the construction sector and rising unemployment.  Thus we continue to forecast that Japanese refined copper consumption will increase by 8.5% this year, to 950kt, and by 5.5% in 2011 to just over 1Mt.  Despite these healthy annual increases demand will still be below the 1.2Mt level reached in 2008.

**China drops two international mining projects from its portfolio of proposed acquisitions** China’s growing appetite in acquiring global copper mining projects has been very much in the news over the past twelve months or so. This has been brought about in order to satisfy its burgeoning smelting and refining base and ultimately its domestic refined copper consumption requirements.  However, over the past few weeks two of these projects have fallen by the wayside and will no longer feature in China’s portfolio of future mines for various reasons.  The first of these occurred in mid June when Quadra FNX Mining Ltd. announced that the memorandum of understanding entered into with State Grid International Development Limited ("SGID") in March 2010 in relation to its 130kt/a Sierra Gorda project had expired with the parties unable to conclude a definitive agreement for the formation of a joint venture.  Seemingly the SGID was not prepared to make a significant financial commitment for feasibility work ahead of the receipt of all necessary permits for the project.  Elsewhere, Zijin Mining Group Co. ended its offer to buy Australia's Indophil Resources NL, partly on account of delays in receiving Chinese Government app

roval for the deal and also because of the passing by local authorities of an environmental code that bans open pit mining in the Philippine province (South Cotabato) in which part of the project is located.  According to local press reports this ban in South Cotabato follows similar directives by local authorities in the Filipino provinces of Marinduque, Mindoro and Palawan.  However, the Philippine Government has condemned these actions declaring that the imposition of such a ban is beyond the scope of authority of local legislation. In December 2009 Zijin entered into a takeover bid of $475M for Indophil to gain access to the 340kt/a Tampakan copper-gold mine which is expected to cost ~$5.2Bn to develop. 

**Mid-year negotiations reach round three in Japan** Last month we noted that mid-year contract negotiations had commenced in earnest and since then BHP Billiton, acting on behalf of Minera Escondida, has completed its third round of discussions with Japanese smelting companies. **Concentrates outlook still bleak for buyers** The chart below illustrates the collapse in copper in concentrate supplies post 2004 when expressed as a percentage of primary smelter capacity.  According to historical precedent, an optimal level of global primary capacity utilisation is 88%.  If copper-in-concentrate availability is in excess of this level then there is a tendency for concentrate stocks to increase within the system, as was the case in 2004 and to a lesser extent in 2005.  However, since then the primary smelting industry has been unable to operate at this optimal rate of 88% due to lack of feed.  Worse still, the combination of disrupted mine output and rapid growth in primary smelter capacity has led to a freefall in copper-in-concentrates supply expressed in the manner above, from a high of almost 94% in 2004 to less than 80% in 2009, and to only 78% implied for 2010.  Measured in absolute tonnage terms the deficits between actual/projected copper in concentrate supplies (after disruptions) and optimal overall industry primary smelter utilisation rates (88%) are 1.4Mt Cu in 2009 and 1.6Mt Cu in 2010.  Note that this larger implied concentrate deficit in 2010 is after allowing for the

removal of smelting capacity at Flin Flon, Kidd Creek and San Luis de Potosi on account of the closure of these plants. In terms of the outlook for the copper concentrate market over the next few years, on the basis of known intentions we expect mine supplies to continue to satisfy just 80% of overall primary smelter capacity requirements, resulting in an implied tonnage gap of more than 1.2Mt/a Cu in both 2011 and 2012. #### **Cu in Concentrate Production as a Percent of Primary Smelting Capacity: 2002 – 2012** 100% 2400
